Ground
GROUND
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ādāmâh and 'erets, Greek gē)
From Old English grund, the bottom or foundation. The Hebrew 'ādāmâh is the tilled, reddish soil, and it stands in a deliberate pun with 'ādām, man: the man is taken from the ground, named for the ground, set to till the ground, cursed in the ground, and returns to the ground. No English rendering can carry the wordplay, but it governs the whole doctrine of man's creaturehood — he is the groundling, and every use of the word in Genesis is pressing that fact upon him.

Biblical Definition

The ground is where man came from, where his curse fell, where he must stand carefully before God, and where the seed of the gospel is either lost or multiplied. Man is formed of it and bound to it, and when he sinned the sentence did not fall on him alone: “cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life” (Gen 3:17). The thorn and the sweated brow are not incidental to the fall; they are the fall written into the soil, so that a man is reminded of his rebellion every time he works. Ground can also be made holy by the presence of God, and the response required is immediate: “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exo 3:5). The bush was in an ordinary wilderness; what sanctified the dirt was who stood in it. In the Lord's parables the ground becomes the heart, and the harvest is decided by what kind of ground the word falls into: “But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience” (Luk 8:15). And the ground is finally the place of the death that produces life, which the Lord applied first of all to Himself: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). Dust, curse, holiness, harvest, and burial — the whole history of man is in this one plain word.

Webster 1828 Definition

The surface of the earth; soil or mould; the land as tilled; and in Scripture the cursed ground of Adam's labour, the holy ground of God's presence, and the good ground of an honest heart receiving the word.

expand to see more

GROUND, n. 1. The surface of the earth or of the terraqueous globe; the earth as we tread upon it.

2. Soil; earth; mould; the substance in which plants take root and grow; as good ground, stony ground.

3. Land; estate; possession; as, he owns a hundred acres of ground.

4. Foundation; that which supports or upholds; hence, the reason or first principle of a thing. The church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. 1 Tim. 3.

5. In Scripture, cursed is the ground for thy sake. Gen. 3. The place whereon thou standest is holy ground. Exod. 3.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:17 — "And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;"

Exodus 3:5 — "And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."

Luke 8:15 — "But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience."

John 12:24 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."

Modern Corruption

The curse on the ground is dismissed as an aetiological myth explaining why farming is hard, severing the connection between human sin and the disordered creation which Romans 8 makes explicit.

expand to see more

The standard modern reading treats Gen 3:17 as an origin-story invented to explain why agriculture is laborious — a pre-scientific people accounting for thorns. On that reading the curse is a description dressed as a sentence, and the moral link between man's rebellion and the world's disorder disappears. Scripture asserts the link as fact and builds doctrine on it: the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope. Paul's whole argument in Rom 8 requires that the groaning of creation be consequent upon Adam's sin and reversible at the revealing of the sons of God. Delete the curse and the promised restoration has nothing to restore, and the resurrection of the body becomes an odd appendix rather than the firstfruits of a renewed earth.

There is a further loss, and it is pastoral. If frustrated labour is simply how the world happens to be, then a man's daily experience of futility — the thorn in every field, the project that will not come right — carries no message. Scripture says it carries a very definite one: it is the ground preaching to the groundling that something is wrong and that he is implicated. That is not a counsel of despair, because the same Scripture sets against Adam's cursed ground the corn of wheat that fell into it willingly and died (Joh 12:24). The ground which swallowed the first man's labour received the last Adam's body, and could not keep it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ādāmâh is tilled soil or ground, punning with 'ādām, man; 'erets is earth or land more broadly. Greek gē is earth, soil, or land, and gives the good ground of the parable of the sower.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ādāmâh (H127) — ground, tilled soil, the reddish earth; man is formed of it (Gen 2:7) and returns to it (Gen 3:19).

Hebrew 'ādām (H120) — man, mankind; the name sounds the ground he was taken from, a pun no translation preserves.

Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, ground in the wider sense of territory rather than soil.

Greek gē (G1093) — earth, soil, ground, land; the ground of the sower's parable, whether stony, thorny, or good.

Greek hedraiōma (G1477) — a stay or support, rendered ground in the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15), a different sense of the English word.

Usage

"Of the curse on man's labour: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it (Gen 3:17)."

"Of ground made holy by God's presence: the place whereon thou standest is holy ground (Exo 3:5)."

"Of the heart receiving the word: that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart... keep it (Luk 8:15)."
